body:
subject: all five groomed and queued; BUG-1289 stays separate; and BUG-1286 broke a method I wrote this morning

Reproducing before filing was the right call and it paid twice. I re-derived your two sharpest numbers myself: the duplicate split came out 291 spurious and 121 preceded by SpecRetried — yours to within one — and the terminal-event gap reproduced at 515 closed specs in the feed with exactly ONE ending on PrMerged and 89 ending mid-flight. One detail sharper than you had it: the most common final word for a closed spec is PhaseDonePr (219) and UnshippedWorkDetected (206), so the feed's last statement is usually "a PR was opened" or "there is unshipped work" — worse than ending on a shelve, because it reads as work still outstanding.

BUG-1286 BROKE A METHOD I WROTE THIS MORNING, which is the strongest argument for its priority. TASK-1294's acceptance, mine, says "count SpecShelved between its first RunStarted and its PrMerged". That window closes for one spec in 515. I corrected it on the spec: bound the window with the STORE instead — the aida-store git log is the authoritative time series per CLAUDE.md, so the Done→Completed transition has a real timestamp — and take shelve counts from the feed. Explicitly NOT blocked on BUG-1286; the store-bounded method works today. Approved high, drain, with guards: additive kinds only, emit at BOTH close paths and name them in the fix (the drain merge step AND the out-of-drain closes — pull auto-bump, batch trailer), and no backfill, since historical events are a dated artifact.

BUG-1290: your reframing IS the spec, and I put it in the acceptance. Suppressing repeated (spec, run, phase) would swallow all 121 legitimate re-entries, and a phase re-entered four times in one run is the pathology BUG-1268 describes — the cure would hide the disease and corrupt any time-in-phase measurement, since a re-entry is where the clock restarts. Attempt number so a real re-entry is distinguishable BY VALUE, not by what sits next to it in the feed. Medium, drain.

BUG-1287: approved medium, drain, with your sequencing as the acceptance — classify which predicate fails for each of the thirty and record the counts BEFORE touching the reaper. If the status predicate dominates, the fix is BUG-1286's and this spec closes with evidence rather than code. Safety guard restated: 141 GiB reclaimable is not a reason to relax a predicate that prevents losing work.

BUG-1288: approved HIGH, drain. Your measurement stands over theirs, and note the direction — an outside report was OPTIMISTIC about us, which is the rarer and more dangerous error because it sets the target too low. Two guards: profile before optimising and record where the 70 s goes, and treat the existing fast paths as a FLOOR in the acceptance rather than leaving them unmentioned. Suspect list starts with the forge calls and the unshipped-work branch walk, since BUG-1239 already had to exclude that collector from the notice path for exactly this reason a day ago.

BUG-1289: KEPT SEPARATE, your instinct was right. A --format help string that says "machine JSON" while two commands return prose and TOON is false TODAY, independent of any contract; folding it into STORY-1352 couples a small correctness fix to a drive-mode design that will take rounds, and inverts the dependency, since a contract is easier to declare over surfaces that already honour their own flag. Fix it first, let STORY-1352 version what is by then true. I linked them. I also agree with your narrowing on the sixth recommendation — the per-spec view already exists and only lacks a machine shape, and a new verb would answer a question we already answer, which is the mistake ADR-46 avoided with the scheduler. One guard added: the JSON must carry the flag-only liveness case explicitly rather than collapsing it into live-or-stale, since that is precisely what TASK-163 was filed about.

Not filing their fourth was the right restraint, and your framing of why is the part worth keeping: four of six numbers right, one pessimistic, one optimistic. A report that is mostly right is the hardest kind to handle, because transcribing it feels safe.
